newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan opposition marks anniversary in disarray.
newsitem.headline: Japan opposition marks anniversary in disarray.

text.p: Japan's largest opposition group marked its second anniversary on Tuesday, but celebrations were overshadowed by last-ditch efforts to stop a key founding member from splitting the fractious and demoralised party.
Shinshinto, or the New Frontier Party (NFP), fared poorly in October general elections, worsening deep personal rivalries within the group.
Party officials on Tuesday tried to persuade former prime minister and party member Tsutomu Hata to drop plans to set up his own political group.
Hata, who headed a fragile minority government for two months in 1994, last week declared he would leave the party in order to forge an opposition alliance against the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).

"This is a grave situation," said NFP Secretary-General Takeo Nishioka. "I will make an appeal for party solidarity and tell him that unity is critical in order to topple the LDP government," he told reporters before meeting with Hata on Tuesday.
Nishioka last week failed to persuade Hata to stay.
Hata has not spelt out his group's policy aims beyond calling for "reform", fuelling speculation that his simmering feud with NFP leader Ichiro Ozawa is the main reason he is quitting.
Hata and Ozawa helped create the NFP but have since clashed over policies, party direction and leadership style.
The party was formed with great fanfare in December 1994 as a merger of nine political groups which made up the reformist governments that ruled Japan briefly from 1993-94.
Leaders sought to make the party a counterweight to the long-ruling LDP following political reforms and realignment that began with the LDP's fall in 1993.

Despite a leadership lineup that includes Hata and two other popular former prime ministers, Toshiki Kaifu and Morihiro Hosokawa, the NFP failed to convince voters it was a viable alternative to an unpopular LDP.

Earlier this year, the NFP looked amateurish when it mounted a parliamentary sit-in as the LDP pushed through an unpopular scheme to use 685 billion yen ($6.06 billion) of taxpayers' money to wind down failed housing mortgage firms.

For general elections in October, Ozawa announced a last-minute policy platform that offered 18 trillion yen ($159 billion) in tax cuts that the LDP attacked as fiscally reckless and analysts dismissed as a desperate electoral ploy.

The NFP paid for those stunts and for public perceptions of party chief Ozawa as high-handed and undemocratic, suffering embarrassing defections and winning only 156 seats in the polls for the 500-seat Lower House of parliament.

Critics say the turmoil sparked by Hata's defection threat is causing the NFP to squander an opportunity to pursue financial scandals at the health and trade ministries that could eventually embroil LDP politicians.
"Far from rising up and taking on the LDP, the party appears to be losing its cohesion day by day and sliding out of control," the daily Asahi Shimbun newspaper said in an editorial. ($=113 yen)
